newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-Japan urged to scrap wetlands project.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Japan urged to scrap wetlands project.

text.p: Scenes of rare mudskipper fish desperately looking for water across miles of parched soil have come to symbolise Japan's hottest environmental row.
Despite some local opposition, the government in April went ahead with a controversial reclamation project in southern Kyushu island, sealing off vast tidal wetlands in western Isahaya Bay.
Two months later, the wetlands, once teeming with hundreds of rare marine species and migrant birds, are slowly dying, prompting protests from around the world.
"We're not against reclamation in principle," said Hirofumi Yamashita, a leading member of Save Isahaya, a local activists' group. "It should be done in stages in the traditional way."
Before April, when the seven-km (four-mile) draining gates came crashing down on the orders of the Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Ministry, protests were confined to local environment groups.

But now, flamed by repeated television reports of the plight of the mudskipper -- an amphibious fish with arm-like fins -- protests are coming from across the country as well as from the World Wide Fund for Nature and the U.S. Ramsar Committee.
Japan has ratified the Ramsar Treaty, which mandates signatories to preserve wetlands used by migrating birds, but Tokyo has designated only one such wetlands in northern Japan.
The row has taken a political spin as well.
Opposition parties have joined the activists in demanding a review of Isahaya and other outdated public works projects.

"If the farm minister won't call off the project, parliament should decide whether he is suitable for his position," Democratic Party leader Naoto Kan said before a group of bipartisan politicians in support of saving Isahaya.
"Opening the draining gates is the first step towards administrative reform," said Social Democrat Tadatoshi Akiba.
LOCAL SUPPORT
But the government has steadfastly refused to give in on grounds that the local farming community had agreed to the project and wildlife would thrive outside the draining gates.
Residents remember a flood in 1957 which killed 680 people and many say the gates will prevent such disasters.
But disaster experts, hired to conduct a study by the Farm Ministry, disagree.
Isahaya farmers, many of them in their 70s, say the gates will free them of the back-breaking chores of upkeeping water outlets and clearing silt that have taxed generations.
"But no one (in Isahaya) dislikes the wetlands. We grew up with this land... It was part of our lives," said another local activist, Kenji Tominaga.
A recent survey by the daily Asahi Shimbun showed 58 percent of those surveyed nationwide, and 54 percent in the Isahaya area, supported opening the draining gates.
OUTDATED PROJECT

The reclamation project to create more rice paddies dates from a 1952 blueprint when Japan was still suffering from food shortages in the aftermath of World War Two. But strong protests from local fishermen delayed the project.

The government revamped the basic plan in the 1970s after a jump in rice production forced Tokyo to pay farmers not to grow rice. The new plan made disaster prevention the main reason, while the reclaimed land was to be used for growing vegetables and dairy farming.

A breakthrough came in the mid-1980s when fishermen agreed to abandon fishing rights and the reclamation area was reduced to the current 3,550 hectares (8,770 acres). The project is expected to be completed by 2000.
PUBLIC WORKS QUESTIONED
The Isahaya case has also put the spotlight on Japan's wasteful public works projects. Often, politicians and bureaucrats refuse to review a plan once it has been put into action.
"The issue in Isahaya is not just about the environment. We are in fact perplexed that all the attention is on the mudskippers and migratory birds," Tominaga said.
"This project has ceased to serve its purpose."
Japan already has substantial paddy fields lying idle, and many doubt that aging local farmers are ready to pay cash to begin farming on newly reclaimed land.
Tominaga said activists and farmers were no longer able to communicate. "It's a kind of mass hysteria here. The only solution we have now is for politics to intervene," he said.
